clue.text: One more than ready to throw a line to one in trouble

definitions.text: One more than ready to throw a line to one in trouble

parts.words: One more than ready to throw a line to one in trouble
parts.note: read first as a comparative, someone readier than ready; then as the theatre helper who feeds a forgotten line to an actor who has dried

explanation.surface: Someone eager to rescue a person in difficulty by tossing them a rope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw a line' suggests a lifebelt and rope, but the line is a line of dialogue fed from the wings; 'more than ready' gives the comparative of prompt.
explanation.definitionFit: In a theatre this person sits offstage and supplies forgotten words to actors; the word is also the comparative of prompt, meaning readier.

clue.text: Danger at sea? Not, it's said, if you shorten sail with it

definitions.text: if you shorten sail with it

parts.note: a reef is a ridge of rock just below the surface, a hazard to ships

indicators.note: tells us the preceding word is only heard, so its spoken form is wanted with a different spelling

parts.note: the word not, which is spoken the same as a tied knot

explanation.surface: A sailor wonders whether shortening sail could be dangerous, and is reassured it is not.
explanation.walkthrough: To reef a sail is to shorten it by tying up part of it, and the knot used is named for that job.
explanation.definitionFit: This flat square knot is the one sailors use when tying in reefs to reduce the area of sail.

clue.text: Gent's wear, £500?

parts.note: looks like a pricey item of menswear; in British slang a monkey is five hundred pounds, and the garment is a short close-fitting jacket

explanation.surface: A shopper balks at a price tag of five hundred pounds on a man's garment.
explanation.walkthrough: British slang calls £500 a 'monkey'; add the garment, a jacket, to get a short tight jacket once worn by sailors and waiters.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a short, close-fitting jacket traditionally worn by sailors or as formal mess dress, an item of men's clothing.

clue.text: "That roars so loud, and — in the index?" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "That roars so loud, and — in the index?" (Hamlet)

parts.words: "That roars so loud, and — in the index?" (Hamlet)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: Queen Gertrude asks what act it is that roars so loud and does this in the index, so the missing verb fills the blank

explanation.surface: A line quoted from Shakespeare's Hamlet with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Gertrude's line in Act 3 Scene 4 runs 'Ay me, what act, That roars so loud and thunders in the index?'; the solver supplies the missing verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation needs a verb paired with roaring, meaning booms loudly like a storm.

clue.text: Tell about Dracula

parts.note: re is a Latin-derived word meaning concerning or on the subject of
Bram Stoker's vampire is a Transylvanian nobleman, Count Dracula

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to give an account of Dracula.
explanation.definitionFit: To tell a story is to narrate it in detail, a synonym of relate.

clue.text: Roger, like Dr Johnson, was tutor to royalty

parts.note: as can mean in the manner of, a synonym of like
Samuel Johnson was nicknamed 'the great Cham' of literature, cham being an old form of khan

explanation.surface: A man called Roger, like Samuel Johnson, once taught members of a royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger Ascham (1515-68) was tutor to the young Elizabeth I; 'was tutor to royalty' confirms the definition. Johnson was dubbed 'the great Cham of literature' by Smollett.
explanation.definitionFit: The forename picks out a Tudor scholar who wrote The Scholemaster and taught Princess Elizabeth.

clue.text: 16 let out on the mountainside

indicators.note: signals that the following word is removed from the cross-referenced answer

parts.note: the answer to 16 across is the colour worn by Will of Robin Hood's band
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something is released onto the slopes of a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let out' looks like a phrase meaning released, but 'let' is the letters removed from 16 across, with 'out' as the deletion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is a steep rocky cliff or bare outcrop on a hillside, a northern English word.

clue.text: Composer sent same for amendment

indicators.note: something put up for amendment is to be altered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A musician's letter was returned unchanged for corrections.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Massenet was a French composer of operas such as Manon and Werther.

clue.text: Girl mixes a sauce with it

indicators.note: a cook who mixes things stirs them together, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A young woman stirs a sauce in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixes' rearranges A SAUCE plus IT; 'with' just joins the two parts of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Eustacia is a female first name, borne by Eustacia Vye in Hardy's The Return of the Native.

clue.text: Little Jock put on the bottle

definitions.meaning: a Scots word for a small child; Jock is slang for a Scotsman
to move a baby from breast milk to other feeding, such as a bottle

explanation.walkthrough: Wean (from 'wee ane', little one) is Scottish dialect for a child; Jock is a nickname for a Scotsman.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a Scottish word for a youngster; the other is the verb meaning to accustom an infant to food other than its mother's milk.

clue.text: Tarts in his court

parts.note: alludes to the nursery rhyme in which the Knave steals the tarts and is tried before this monarch in Alice in Wonderland

explanation.surface: Disreputable women frequent a nobleman's household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tarts' suggests loose women, but these are pastries from the rhyme 'The Queen of Hearts, she made some tarts'; the trial over them is held in this ruler's court in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lewis Carroll's story the playing-card monarch presides at the trial of the Knave for stealing pastries.

clue.text: Among the ferns the voice of summer?

parts.note: read as one who sums, a calculator; with a possessive, an adder's
tongue can mean language or the power of speech, a sense of voice

explanation.surface: Botanical musing: is there a summer voice to be heard among the ferns?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summer' is the season on the surface but here means someone who adds up. The definition says the answer is one of the ferns.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a small fern, Ophioglossum, whose spore-bearing spike resembles a snake's tongue.

clue.text: Recover from frenzy — merely use protein catalyst

indicators.note: the letters are to be retrieved from inside the following words, spanning the gap between them

explanation.surface: Advice to get over a rage by simply using a biochemical agent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recover from' looks like advice about getting over something, but it asks you to extract the run of letters across 'frenzy merely'.
explanation.definitionFit: Such substances are proteins that speed up chemical reactions in living things.

clue.text: Old Algerian or, say, new son of Abraham

indicators.note: signals a spoken form, so the word new is wanted spelt as it is pronounced

parts.note: the word new, which sounds like the Greek letter nu
Midian was a son of Abraham by Keturah in Genesis

explanation.surface: A North African of long ago, or perhaps a fresh descendant of the patriarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Numidia was an ancient Berber kingdom covering much of what is now Algeria.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of ancient Numidia, a kingdom of North Africa in the territory of modern Algeria.

clue.text: Music-maker in some ways right out of Germany

indicators.note: the right and German pieces are placed within the abbreviation for streets

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way, so two of them give STS
aus is the German word for out

explanation.surface: A composer who has fled his homeland in various ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of Germany' reads as emigration but means the German word for 'out'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Strauss family, and Richard Strauss, were composers, makers of waltzes and operas.

clue.text: Trims up with him, joining top-class fliers

indicators.note: in a down clue the word is read upwards, so its letters are taken in reverse

parts.note: pares means trims or cuts back
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man smartens himself up and joins an elite group of pilots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fliers' suggests pilots or birds, but these winged beings are angels; in a down clue 'up' reads the trimming word bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the highest order of angels, winged beings in the celestial hierarchy.

clue.text: Will however we see him in Lincoln green?

definitions.text: Will however we see him in Lincoln green?

parts.words: Will however we see him in Lincoln green?
parts.note: Robin Hood's men wore Lincoln green cloth, yet one of them has a colour for a surname, a red one, which makes the question a paradox

explanation.surface: Asking whether a man named Will appears dressed in Lincoln green.
explanation.walkthrough: Will Scarlet is one of Robin Hood's merry men, who dressed in Lincoln green; the joke is a red name on a green-clad man.
explanation.definitionFit: The outlaw companion of Robin Hood bears a surname that is a bright red colour.

clue.text: RAMC staff somewhat mercurial

parts.note: the RAMC, Royal Army Medical Corps, uses a medical staff as an emblem, and the snake-twined wand also belongs to the god Mercury

explanation.surface: Army medical personnel described as rather volatile in temperament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like personnel but is a rod; 'mercurial' means belonging to Mercury, whose wand this is, often used as a medical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: This winged wand twined with two snakes was carried by Mercury and is widely used as an emblem of medicine.

clue.text: Even when disturbed, run to find cover

indicators.note: something disturbed is thrown out of order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: to lope is to run with a long easy stride

explanation.surface: Even when disturbed, someone runs off to hide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disturbed' rearranges the letters of 'Even'; 'when' and 'to find' are link words. 'Cover' is a noun here, the paper wrapping for a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: This paper wrapper encloses a letter, so it serves as a cover.

clue.text: Performed aerobatics when underdeveloped

definitions.meaning: did tricks in an aircraft, such as loops and rolls
checked in growth, not reaching full size

explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the past tense of doing flying tricks; the other is an adjective for growth that has been held back.

clue.text: It's not in your cellar but could be in mine

definitions.text: It's not in your cellar but could be in mine

parts.words: It's not in your cellar but could be in mine
parts.note: read as a boast about one's wine cellar, but a salt cellar holds table salt, while a mine may yield the mineral form

explanation.surface: A host tells a guest their cellar lacks something his own might hold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cellar' suggests wine, but means a salt cellar; 'mine' looks like a possessive but is a pit from which the mineral is dug.
explanation.definitionFit: Halite, the mineral form of sodium chloride, is extracted from mines, unlike refined table salt.

clue.text: Scottish antipodes?

parts.note: a question about what lies far from Scotland's southern opposite: the polar region nearest Scotland, opposite the southern pole

explanation.surface: A question about what lies on the far side of the world from Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: The far-north polar region is the opposite pole to the far south; the precise Scottish link in this old clue is obscure.
explanation.definitionFit: The polar region of the far north lies opposite the southern polar region on the globe.

clue.text: Receiver appears in this case

parts.note: a legal or bankruptcy reading is suggested, but in grammar the recipient, the indirect object, takes a particular case

explanation.surface: An official receiver turns up in a legal dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Receiver' suggests an official handling bankruptcy and 'case' a lawsuit; in grammar, this case marks the indirect object, the one given to.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin and German grammar this noun case marks the indirect object, the person to whom something is given.

clue.text: Chin can't open? Maybe get things moving with this

indicators.note: suggests the preceding words could be a different arrangement of letters

explanation.surface: A jaw that won't open; perhaps something will shift it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' rearranges all of CHIN CANT OPEN; 'get things moving' is a furniture van, not a cure.
explanation.definitionFit: This large furniture removal van is used to transport household goods when people move house.

clue.text: Gas light

definitions.meaning: an inert element found in the air
a glowing advertising tube filled with this element

explanation.definitionFit: It is a noble gaseous element, and also the name for the glowing tube signs it fills.

clue.text: One is inclined to have such a mind

definitions.text: One is inclined to have such a mind

parts.words: One is inclined to have such a mind
parts.note: refers to the idiom of having half a mind or this kind of mind to do something, meaning being strongly inclined

explanation.surface: A remark that one tends to have a certain kind of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'have a good mind to' do something is to be strongly inclined to do it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom having a good mind to means feeling a strong inclination.

clue.text: Edmund joins the club team

parts.note: an iron is a type of golf club
a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: A man named Edmund signs up with a sports club's team.
explanation.walkthrough: Edmund Ironside was King of England briefly in 1016.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anglo-Saxon king Edmund II was nicknamed for his valour against the Danes.

clue.text: East Anglian town always cut in two

parts.note: Diss is a market town in Norfolk, in the east of England
ever means at all times, always

explanation.surface: A town in eastern England is permanently divided.
explanation.walkthrough: Diss is a small market town in Norfolk, East Anglia.
explanation.definitionFit: To dissever is to sever or split apart, an old word for dividing.
